moments.title: Eigenvalues, eigenvectors and matrix powers
moments.text: The video focuses on using eigenvalues and eigenvectors to express powers of a matrix.

moments.title: An invariant direction
moments.text: A diagram compares transformed vectors. An eigenvector is mapped onto its own span, with its eigenvalue giving the scalar multiplier.

moments.title: Labels for eigenvalues and eigenvectors
moments.text: The presenter labels eigenvalues with $\lambda$ and associates each with a corresponding eigenvector.

moments.title: Diagonalisation and powers
moments.text: For a matrix with a suitable eigenvector basis, write $M=PDP^{-1}$ and $M^n=PD^nP^{-1}$, with corresponding eigenvectors and eigenvalues in matching order.

moments.title: Find eigenvalues
moments.text: The presenter uses a TI-Nspire to compute eigenvalues of the example matrix.

moments.title: Characteristic equation
moments.text: Eigenvalues are also found by solving $\det(\lambda I-M)=0$.

moments.title: Find eigenvectors
moments.text: For each eigenvalue, find a corresponding nonzero vector satisfying $(M-\lambda I)\mathbf v=\mathbf0$.

moments.title: Calculator eigenvectors and inverse
moments.text: The video stores a calculator-generated eigenvector matrix $P$ and obtains $P^{-1}$.

moments.title: An eigenvector by hand
moments.text: Substitute the first eigenvalue into the eigenvector equation and solve for a nonzero vector.

moments.title: Scalar multiples
moments.text: Nonzero scalar multiples represent equally valid eigenvectors for the same eigenvalue.

moments.title: Assemble the power formula
moments.text: The presenter combines the eigenvalues, eigenvector matrix and its inverse to form an expression for $M^n$.

moments.title: Calculate a fourth power
moments.text: The video substitutes $n=4$ and compares diagonalisation with a direct calculator matrix power.

moments.title: Why keep a formula for n?
moments.text: A general expression in $n$ can help analyse repeated transformations or long-term behaviour, not just one numerical power.

notes.title: Conditions and matching
notes.text: The power formula requires an invertible eigenvector matrix. The diagonal entry and eigenvector in each corresponding position must describe the same eigenpair.
notes.write: For the syllabus's distinct-real-eigenvalue case, put each eigenvector in a column of $P$ and its matching eigenvalue in the same position on $D$.

notes.title: Sign and zero eigenvalues
notes.text: The opening visual focuses on stretching along a line. An eigenvalue can also be negative or zero.
notes.write: A negative eigenvalue reverses direction; a zero eigenvalue maps the eigenvector to the zero vector. The eigenvector itself must be nonzero.

moments.title: Matrix tools on the calculator
moments.text: The presenter demonstrates matrix creation and operations on a TI-Nspire.

moments.title: Create a matrix
moments.text: A 2-by-2 matrix is entered and stored for later use.

moments.title: Arithmetic operations
moments.text: The stored matrix is reused for addition, subtraction, multiplication and a power.

moments.title: Determinant and inverse
moments.text: The video finds the determinant and then uses the inverse operation on the stored matrix.

moments.title: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors
moments.text: The final portion moves to calculator commands for eigenvalues and eigenvectors, which connect to AHL 1.15.

moments.title: Interpreting an eigenvector
moments.text: The presenter notes that a calculator may return a different scalar multiple of an eigenvector.

moments.title: Continue practising
moments.text: The video recommends practising entry, storage and operations with matrices.

notes.title: Calculator shown
notes.text: This demonstration uses a TI-Nspire. Its menus and commands differ from the Casio fx-CG50.
notes.write: Use the correct matrix editor and operation commands for your calculator, and check dimensions and output.

ican.text: I can explain an eigenvalue and a nonzero eigenvector using $A\mathbf v=\lambda\mathbf v$.
I can form and solve the characteristic equation for a 2-by-2 matrix.
I can find and check an eigenvector for each eigenvalue.
I can diagonalise a 2-by-2 matrix with distinct real eigenvalues, matching eigenvectors to diagonal entries.
I can use $A^n=PD^nP^{-1}$ and check a particular power using technology.
I can interpret eigenvalues in a repeated-transformation context.

ku.text: An eigenvector $\mathbf v$ is nonzero and satisfies $A\mathbf v=\lambda\mathbf v$. The eigenvalue $\lambda$ is the scalar multiplier associated with that vector.
A negative eigenvalue reverses the direction of a nonzero eigenvector; an eigenvalue of zero maps it to the zero vector. Zero is not an eigenvector.
Find eigenvalues from $\det(A-\lambda I)=0$. For each eigenvalue, solve $(A-\lambda I)\mathbf v=\mathbf0$ and choose a nonzero vector in the solution set.
Every nonzero scalar multiple of an eigenvector for $\lambda$ is also an eigenvector for $\lambda$. A calculator's normalized vector may look different from an exact integer multiple.

When $A$ has two distinct real eigenvalues, choose corresponding eigenvectors as columns of $P$ and place their eigenvalues in the matching diagonal positions of $D$. Then $A=PDP^{-1}$ and $A^n=PD^nP^{-1}$ for nonnegative integers $n$.
For $D=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\lambda_2)$, $D^n=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1^n,\lambda_2^n)$. Check $AP=PD$ before using the power formula.
Preserve exact eigenvectors or sufficient calculator precision; rounding matrix entries early can make a correct power appear inaccurate.

misc.weak: The zero vector is an eigenvector because $A\mathbf0=\lambda\mathbf0$.
misc.better: Eigenvectors must be nonzero. The zero vector satisfies the equation for every scalar and identifies no eigendirection.

misc.weak: If an eigenvector has negative entries it cannot be correct.
misc.better: Any nonzero scalar multiple is valid, including one that reverses the sign of every entry.

misc.weak: The first column of $P$ can be paired with either diagonal entry of $D$.
misc.better: Match each eigenvector column to its own eigenvalue in the corresponding diagonal position.

misc.weak: A negative eigenvalue means the matrix has no real eigenvectors.
misc.better: A real negative eigenvalue can have real eigenvectors; it reverses their direction under the transformation.

misc.weak: Every 2-by-2 matrix can be diagonalised using two eigenvectors.
misc.better: Diagonalisation requires an eigenvector basis. The syllabus calculation here is restricted to distinct real eigenvalues, which provide two independent eigenvectors.

terms.text: Form the characteristic equation and solve for the allowed eigenvalues.
Substitute an eigenvalue into $(A-\lambda I)\mathbf v=\mathbf0$, then give a nonzero solution.
Construct $P$ and $D$ in matching order and verify $AP=PD$ and that $P$ is invertible.
Raise each diagonal entry of $D$ to the requested power, then calculate $PD^nP^{-1}$ in order.

formula.text: For $A=PDP^{-1}$, the booklet gives $A^n=PD^nP^{-1}$, where the columns of $P$ are eigenvectors and $D$ is the corresponding diagonal matrix of eigenvalues.

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Find one eigenvector for each eigenvalue.
parts.a: For $\lambda=4$, one choice is $\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}$. For $\lambda=2$, one choice is $\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}$. Both are nonzero and satisfy $A\mathbf v=\lambda\mathbf v$.

parts.label: (c)
parts.a: A matching choice is $P=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$ and $D=\begin{pmatrix}4&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$. Here $P^{-1}=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$.

kq.q: Why can two eigenvectors for the same eigenvalue look different?
kq.model: Any nonzero scalar multiple of a particular eigenvector is another eigenvector for the same eigenvalue, so a calculator's normalized output may differ by a scale factor.

kq.q: Why must the eigenvalues in $D$ be matched to the columns of $P$?
kq.model: The equation $AP=PD$ means each column of $AP$ must be the corresponding column of $P$ multiplied by its own diagonal entry.

kq.q: What does a zero eigenvalue mean geometrically?
kq.model: A nonzero eigenvector associated with it is mapped to the zero vector by the transformation.

kq.q: Why can diagonalisation simplify a general matrix power?
kq.model: Powers of a diagonal matrix are found by raising its diagonal entries to the power. The matrices $P$ and $P^{-1}$ change coordinates into and out of the eigenvector basis.
